statement: Points P, Q, R and S lie on a straight line, not necessarily in that order. PQ = 7, QR = 3, RS = 5 and PS = 9. What is the distance PR?

choices.misconception: I subtracted QR from PS, thinking PR is the whole of PS except the stretch from Q to R.
I assumed the points were in alphabetical order along the line, so I added PQ and QR.
I placed S between P and R, so I added PS and SR.
I assumed alphabetical order and added all three gaps, finding the full length instead of PR.

hints: Put P at 0 on a number line and place the others.
Draw a number line with P at zero. Q is forced to sit at distance 7, then try both sides for R, and both sides for S, keeping only the placement that matches the last given length.
With P at 0 and Q at 7, R is at 10 or 4. From R = 10, S would be at 15 or 5, never 9 away from P. From R = 4, S can be at 9.

solutions.reliable: Place P at 0 and Q at 7 (the mirror image gives the same distances). Then R is at 10 or at 4. If R = 10, S is at 15 or 5, and neither is 9 from P. If R = 4, S is at 9 or -1, and S = 9 fits PS = 9. So the order is P, R, Q, S and PR = 4. The transferable idea: when the order of points is not given, a quick number line turns guessing into checking.
solutions.elegant: PS = 9 is less than PQ + QR + RS = 15, so the points cannot be in alphabetical order. Drawing it shows R doubles back between P and Q.

whyOnTest: Distance puzzles on a line are about not assuming the order of the letters, and drawing the line exposes the one arrangement that fits.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
